intro: Hi! Today you learn to put two ideas into one smooth sentence with who, which, that and where: the colleague who sits next to me, the app that I use every day, the office where I work. You already do this in Indonesian with 'yang'. Warm-up: how would you say 'teman yang tinggal di Bandung' in English?
teachingNotes: A defining relative clause tells us WHICH person, thing or place we mean (the man who lives next door). Bridge from Indonesian 'yang': yang + person = who (or that), yang + thing/animal = which (or that), 'tempat' (kantor tempat saya bekerja) = where. that works for people AND things, so never test who vs that or which vs that as competing options: both are correct. Test who vs which, where vs which, the doubled object and leaving the pronoun out. Never accept 'what' as a relative pronoun (*the phone what I bought).
Common error 1: which for people (*The man which lives next door is a doctor → who). which is only for things and animals (pets are sometimes who; only mention it if asked).

Common error 2: repeating the thing (*This is the book that I bought it yesterday). that/which already stands for the book, so the place after bought stays empty. Indonesian works the same way (buku yang saya beli, not *buku yang saya beli buku itu); learners add it because a normal English sentence needs it (I bought it). The same with the subject: *The man who he lives next door.

Common error 3: which for a place where English needs where (*That's the office which I work → where I work). Test: if you can say 'there' in the small sentence (I work there), use where + person + verb. If the place does the action or is the thing you visit, buy or like (The mall opened last month / I visited the city), use which or that: the mall which opened last month, the city which I visited. 'the office which I work in' is also correct (a note only; don't drill prepositions at the end).

Leaving out the pronoun: look at the word after who/which/that. If a person or thing comes next (I bought, my boss sent, we ordered), the pronoun is the object and can be dropped: the book I bought. If a verb comes next (lives, works, fixed), it is the subject and must stay: the man who lives next door, never *the man lives next door. Indonesian always says 'yang', so learners think dropping it is wrong; it is normal, especially when speaking. Don't drop where in this lesson.

Limits: defining clauses only. No commas / non-defining clauses, no whose, whom or when as a relative word, no passive or past perfect in examples. 'yang + adjective' is NOT a relative clause in English: rumah yang besar = a big house (not *a house which big), yang merah = the red one. neighbour (British) / neighbor (American); that is more common than which in everyday speech, especially in American English.

keyPoints.title: Join two ideas into one sentence
keyPoints.explanation: A relative clause is the 'yang …' part that tells us which person, thing or place you mean. Put it right after the noun: I have a friend. She works in a bank. → I have a friend who works in a bank. who/which/that already stands for the person or thing, so don't repeat it: the book that I bought (not 'that I bought it').

examples.en: I have a friend who works in a bank.
examples.id: Saya punya teman yang bekerja di bank.

examples.en: The food that we ordered was cold.
examples.id: Makanan yang kami pesan dingin. (bukan 'that we ordered it')

id.title: Menggabungkan dua ide jadi satu kalimat
id.explanation: Relative clause adalah bagian 'yang …' yang menjelaskan orang, benda atau tempat mana yang kamu maksud. Taruh tepat setelah kata bendanya: I have a friend. She works in a bank. → I have a friend who works in a bank. who/which/that sudah mewakili orang atau benda itu, jadi jangan diulang: the book that I bought (bukan 'that I bought it').

keyPoints.title: who, which, that or where
keyPoints.explanation: who = people. which = things and animals (never people). that = people or things, very common when speaking. where = places, followed by a person + verb (the office where I work). If the place itself does the action or is the thing you visit or like, use which or that: the mall which opened last month.

examples.en: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
examples.id: Pria yang tinggal di sebelah rumah adalah dokter.

examples.en: This is the bus which goes to the airport.
That's the office where I work.

id.title: who, which, that atau where
id.explanation: who = orang. which = benda dan hewan (tidak pernah untuk orang). that = orang atau benda, sangat umum saat bicara. where = tempat, diikuti orang + kata kerja (the office where I work). Kalau tempat itu sendiri yang melakukan sesuatu atau yang kamu kunjungi/sukai, pakai which atau that: the mall which opened last month.

keyPoints.title: Leave out who, which or that when it's the object
keyPoints.explanation: Look at the word after who/which/that. If another person or thing comes next (I, we, my boss + verb), you can leave the pronoun out: the book I bought. If a verb comes next, it must stay: the man who lives next door (not 'the man lives next door').

examples.en: The song you sang at the party was great.
examples.id: Lagu yang kamu nyanyikan di pesta itu bagus sekali. (that boleh hilang)

examples.en: The driver who took me home was very kind.
examples.id: Sopir yang mengantar saya pulang sangat baik. (who wajib ada)

id.title: Menghilangkan who, which atau that saat ia berfungsi sebagai objek
id.explanation: Lihat kata setelah who/which/that. Kalau setelahnya ada orang atau benda lain (I, we, my boss + kata kerja), kata penghubungnya boleh dihilangkan: the book I bought. Kalau setelahnya langsung kata kerja, kata itu wajib ada: the man who lives next door (bukan 'the man lives next door').

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with who or which: The train ___ goes to Bogor is very crowded in the morning.
guidedPractice.hint: A train is a thing, not a person.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with where or which: That's the warung ___ we always eat lunch.
guidedPractice.hint: Can you say 'we always eat lunch there'?

guidedPractice.prompt: Join the two sentences with who: I met a woman. She works at a hospital in Surabaya.
expected: i met a woman who works at a hospital in surabaya
i met a woman that works at a hospital in surabaya
guidedPractice.hint: who replaces she. Don't keep she.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write the sentence again without that: The film that we watched last night was boring.
expected: the film we watched last night was boring
guidedPractice.hint: After that comes 'we', so that is the object and can go.

independentPractice.prompt: Correct the mistake: The cake that my mother made it was delicious.
expected: the cake that my mother made was delicious
the cake which my mother made was delicious
the cake my mother made was delicious
independentPractice.hint: that already means 'the cake'. Don't say it twice.

independentPractice.prompt: Complete with one word: The hospital ___ my sister works is near the station.
Join the two sentences without who, which or that: Here is the recipe. My grandmother wrote it.
expected: here is the recipe my grandmother wrote
here's the recipe my grandmother wrote
independentPractice.hint: Drop 'it' too: the recipe already is the thing she wrote.

assessment.prompt: Complete with one word: I need a phone ___ has a good camera.
assessment.rubric: Correct: which or that (a phone is a thing). 'who' = 20 (who is for people). 'where' or 'what' = 0. Leaving it empty = 0 (a verb comes next, so the word must stay).

assessment.prompt: Complete with one word: Pak Hasan is the doctor ___ helped my mother at the hospital.
assessment.rubric: Correct: who or that (a doctor is a person). 'which' = 30 (which is not for people). 'where' or 'what' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete with one word: Yogyakarta is the city ___ I grew up.
assessment.rubric: Correct: where (I grew up there). 'which' or 'that' = 20 (they would need 'in' at the end: which I grew up in). 'who' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Join the two sentences into one with who, which or that: I have a neighbour. She sells nasi uduk every morning.
acceptableAnswers: i have a neighbour who sells nasi uduk every morning
i have a neighbor who sells nasi uduk every morning
i have a neighbour that sells nasi uduk every morning
i have a neighbor that sells nasi uduk every morning
assessment.rubric: Correct: I have a neighbour who (or that) sells nasi uduk every morning. 'who she sells' = 40 (she is repeated). 'which sells' = 50 (which is not for people). 'I have a neighbour sells…' without who = 30. Two separate sentences = 0.

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: The bag that I left it on the KRL was brand new.
acceptableAnswers: the bag that i left on the krl was brand new
the bag which i left on the krl was brand new
the bag i left on the krl was brand new
assessment.rubric: Correct: remove 'it' (that already means the bag): The bag that I left on the KRL was brand new. Also accept which or no pronoun. Removing 'that' but keeping 'it' = 20. No change = 0.

assessment.prompt: Join the two sentences without who, which or that: This is the laptop. I bought it last week.
acceptableAnswers: this is the laptop i bought last week
assessment.rubric: Correct: This is the laptop I bought last week. With that or which = 60 (correct English, but the task was to leave it out). Keeping 'it' (…I bought it last week) = 20. 'This is the laptop who…' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: The nurse looked after my father was very patient.
acceptableAnswers: the nurse who looked after my father was very patient
the nurse that looked after my father was very patient
assessment.rubric: Correct: add who (or that) after nurse: a verb (looked after) comes next, so the word can't be left out. 'which looked after' = 50 (which is not for people). No change = 0.

blocks.text: Two short sentences can become one: *I have a colleague. She speaks Japanese.* → *I have a colleague **who speaks Japanese**.* The part in bold is a **relative clause**: a small sentence that tells us **which** person, thing or place you mean. The word that starts it (**who, which, that, where**) is like Indonesian **yang**. Notice that **who** takes the place of **she**: you don't keep both.

id.text: Dua kalimat pendek bisa jadi satu: *I have a colleague. She speaks Japanese.* → *I have a colleague **who speaks Japanese**.* Bagian yang tebal disebut **relative clause**: kalimat kecil yang menjelaskan orang, benda atau tempat **yang mana** yang kamu maksud. Kata pembukanya (**who, which, that, where**) mirip **yang** dalam bahasa Indonesia. Perhatikan: **who** menggantikan **she**, jadi jangan pakai keduanya.

rows.en: I have a friend who works in a bank.
rows.id: Saya punya teman yang bekerja di bank.

rows.en: Do you know a restaurant that sells good rendang?
rows.id: Kamu tahu restoran yang jual rendang enak?

rows.en: That's the office where I work.

blocks.text: Not every **yang** is a relative clause. *rumah yang besar* is just **a big house** (adjective before the noun, as you learnt), not *'a house which big'*. And *yang merah* is **the red one**.

id.text: Tidak semua **yang** jadi relative clause. *rumah yang besar* cukup **a big house** (kata sifat di depan kata benda, seperti yang sudah kamu pelajari), bukan *'a house which big'*. Dan *yang merah* adalah **the red one**.

blocks.prompt: The man who lives next door is a doctor. Which words tell us which man?
blocks.explain: who lives next door is the relative clause: it tells us which man we mean (the one next door, not another man).

id.prompt: The man who lives next door is a doctor. Kata-kata mana yang menjelaskan pria yang mana?
id.explain: who lives next door adalah relative clause-nya: bagian itu menjelaskan pria yang mana yang dimaksud (yang di sebelah rumah, bukan pria lain).

material.title: People and things: who, which, that

blocks.text:
Indonesian has one word, **yang**, for everything. English chooses:
- **who** for **people**: *the woman who cuts my hair*
- **which** for **things and animals**: *the bus which goes to the airport*
- **that** for **people or things**: *the girl that sits next to me*, *the app that I use*. It's very common when speaking, especially in American English.
So for a person you can say **who** or **that**, and for a thing **which** or **that**. Both are correct.

id.text:
Bahasa Indonesia punya satu kata, **yang**, untuk semuanya. Bahasa Inggris memilih:
- **who** untuk **orang**: *the woman who cuts my hair*
- **which** untuk **benda dan hewan**: *the bus which goes to the airport*
- **that** untuk **orang maupun benda**: *the girl that sits next to me*, *the app that I use*. Sangat umum saat bicara, terutama di bahasa Inggris Amerika.
Jadi untuk orang kamu bisa pakai **who** atau **that**, dan untuk benda **which** atau **that**. Keduanya benar.

rows.en: The girl that sits next to me is from Medan.
rows.id: Cewek yang duduk di sebelah saya berasal dari Medan.

rows.en: This is the bus which goes to the airport.
We have a cat which sleeps all day.
rows.id: Kami punya kucing yang tidur seharian.

blocks.text:
Two mistakes to avoid:
- **which** for a person: *'The man which lives next door'* ✗ → *The man **who** lives next door* ✓.
- **what** in the middle of a sentence: *'the phone what I bought'* ✗ → *the phone **that** I bought* ✓. what is for questions (*What did you buy?*), not for 'yang'.

id.text:
Dua kesalahan yang perlu dihindari:
- **which** untuk orang: *'The man which lives next door'* ✗ → *The man **who** lives next door* ✓.
- **what** di tengah kalimat: *'the phone what I bought'* ✗ → *the phone **that** I bought* ✓. what dipakai untuk pertanyaan (*What did you buy?*), bukan untuk 'yang'.

blocks.prompt: I'm looking for a charger ___ works with this phone.
blocks.explain: A charger is a thing, so use which (that is also fine). who is only for people, and where is for places.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: I'm looking for a charger ___ works with this phone.
id.explain: Charger adalah benda, jadi pakai which (that juga boleh). who hanya untuk orang, dan where untuk tempat.

id.title: Orang dan benda: who, which, that

blocks.text:
For a place, Indonesian often says **tempat**: *kantor tempat saya bekerja*. English uses **where**, followed by a person + verb: *the office **where I work***. Saying *'the office which I work'* is a common mistake.
**The trick:** make the small sentence with **there**. *I work there* ✓ → **where**. But if the place itself does something, or is the thing you visit, like or buy, there is no 'there': *The mall opened last month* → *the mall **which** opened last month*; *I visited the city* → *the city **which** I visited*.

id.text:
Untuk tempat, bahasa Indonesia sering memakai **tempat**: *kantor tempat saya bekerja*. Bahasa Inggris memakai **where**, diikuti orang + kata kerja: *the office **where I work***. Bilang *'the office which I work'* adalah kesalahan yang sering terjadi.
**Triknya:** buat kalimat kecilnya dengan **there** (di sana). *I work there* ✓ → **where**. Tapi kalau tempat itu sendiri yang melakukan sesuatu, atau tempat itu yang kamu kunjungi, sukai atau beli, tidak ada 'there': *The mall opened last month* → *the mall **which** opened last month*; *I visited the city* → *the city **which** I visited*.

rows.en: That's the office where I work.
This is the school where my kids study.
rows.id: Ini sekolah tempat anak-anak saya belajar.

rows.en: Let's go to the mall which opened last month.
rows.id: Ayo ke mal yang baru buka bulan lalu.

blocks.text: You may also see *the office **which** I work **in***: which + the little word **in** at the end. It's correct too, but **where I work** is shorter and more common. For now, use **where**.

id.text: Kamu mungkin juga melihat *the office **which** I work **in***: which + kata kecil **in** di akhir. Itu juga benar, tapi **where I work** lebih pendek dan lebih umum. Untuk sekarang, pakai **where**.

blocks.prompt: That's the gym ___ Dimas trains every evening.
blocks.explain: Dimas trains there, so use where. 'which Dimas trains' is missing 'in', and who is for people.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: That's the gym ___ Dimas trains every evening.
id.explain: Dimas berlatih di sana (there), jadi pakai where. 'which Dimas trains' kurang kata 'in', dan who untuk orang.

blocks.text:
In a normal sentence, *bought* needs a thing after it: *I bought **it***. But in *the book **that** I bought*, **that** already means *the book*, so the place after *bought* stays **empty**.
Indonesian works the same way: you say *buku yang saya beli*, not *'buku yang saya beli buku itu'*. So don't add **it**, **him**, **her** or **them**: *'the book that I bought it'* ✗.
The same for the person who does the action: *'the man who **he** lives next door'* ✗. who already means *the man*.

id.text:
Dalam kalimat biasa, *bought* butuh benda setelahnya: *I bought **it***. Tapi di *the book **that** I bought*, **that** sudah berarti *the book*, jadi tempat setelah *bought* dibiarkan **kosong**.
Bahasa Indonesia juga begitu: kita bilang *buku yang saya beli*, bukan *'buku yang saya beli buku itu'*. Jadi jangan tambahkan **it**, **him**, **her** atau **them**: *'the book that I bought it'* ✗.
Sama juga untuk pelakunya: *'the man who **he** lives next door'* ✗. who sudah berarti *the man*.

rows.en: This is the book that I bought yesterday.
rows.id: Ini buku yang saya beli kemarin.

rows.en: The email that Rina sent was very long.
rows.id: Email yang dikirim Rina panjang sekali.

rows.en: The people that we invited are all here.
rows.id: Orang-orang yang kami undang sudah datang semua.

options: The photos that you took them in Bali are beautiful.
The photos that you took in Bali are beautiful.
blocks.explain: that already means 'the photos', so don't add them after took.

id.explain: that sudah berarti 'the photos', jadi jangan tambahkan them setelah took.

material.title: Leaving out who, which or that

blocks.text:
Indonesian always keeps **yang**. English can often drop the word, especially when speaking. **The trick: look at the word right after who/which/that.**
- A **person or thing + verb** comes next (*I bought, we ordered, my boss sent*): the word is the **object** (the thing that receives the action, *yang dikenai*). You **can leave it out**: *the book **I** bought*.
- A **verb** comes next (*lives, works, took*): the word is the **subject** (the one who does the action, *pelakunya*). It **must stay**: *the man **who lives** next door*, never *'the man lives next door'*.

id.text:
Bahasa Indonesia selalu memakai **yang**. Bahasa Inggris sering boleh menghilangkannya, terutama saat bicara. **Triknya: lihat kata tepat setelah who/which/that.**
- Kalau setelahnya ada **orang atau benda + kata kerja** (*I bought, we ordered, my boss sent*): kata itu adalah **objek** (yang dikenai pekerjaan). Kamu **boleh menghilangkannya**: *the book **I** bought*.
- Kalau setelahnya langsung **kata kerja** (*lives, works, took*): kata itu adalah **subjek** (pelakunya). Kata itu **wajib ada**: *the man **who lives** next door*, bukan *'the man lives next door'*.

rows.en: The food we ordered was cold.
rows.note: we comes next → that can go

rows.en: The song you sang at the party was great.
rows.id: Lagu yang kamu nyanyikan di pesta itu bagus sekali.
rows.note: you comes next → that can go

rows.en: The driver who took me home was very kind.
rows.id: Sopir yang mengantar saya pulang sangat baik.
rows.note: took comes next → who must stay

blocks.prompt: In which sentence can you leave out who or that?
options: The teacher who taught me English lives in Bogor.
The teacher that my son likes lives in Bogor.
blocks.explain: In the second sentence 'my son' comes after that, so that is the object and can go: The teacher my son likes. In the first, a verb (taught) comes next, so who must stay.

id.prompt: Di kalimat mana kamu boleh menghilangkan who atau that?
id.explain: Di kalimat kedua, setelah that ada 'my son', jadi that adalah objek dan boleh hilang: The teacher my son likes. Di kalimat pertama, setelahnya langsung kata kerja (taught), jadi who wajib ada.

suggestedQuestions: Is 'that' always OK instead of who or which?
Why can't I say 'the book that I bought it'?
When do I use where and when do I use which for a place?
How do I know if I can leave out who, which or that?
